beats.say: Right now, a machine built in 1977 is about to become the first human-made object one full light-day from Earth.
A radio message sent to it today travels for about twenty-four hours, at the speed of light, before it arrives.
And the strangest part is not the distance. It is that the machine is still alive, still listening, and still answering.
It runs on a fading nuclear heat source, computers with less memory than one photo on your phone, and a radio about as strong as a fridge light bulb.
This is Voyager 1. So how is it still alive?
To find out, we have to go back to the summer of 1977.
In the 1960s, mission designers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory noticed something rare. In the late 1970s, the outer planets would line up.
That alignment comes around about once every hundred and seventy-five years. A probe could swing from one giant planet to the next, stealing speed from each.
NASA built two identical probes. Voyager 2 launched first. Voyager 1 followed sixteen days later, on September 5th, 1977.
Voyager 1 took a faster path, and by December it had overtaken its twin.
In March 1979 it swept past Jupiter, about two hundred and eighty thousand kilometers away.
It found a faint ring around the giant planet, and two small moons no one had ever seen.
Jupiter's gravity bent its path and flung it on toward Saturn, faster than before.
In November 1980 it reached Saturn, and the team made a choice that sealed its fate.
They steered it close past Titan, Saturn's largest moon, and the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
It passed about six and a half thousand kilometers from Titan's center, and saw an orange haze over air that is mostly nitrogen.
But that swing past Titan threw Voyager 1 up and out of the plane of the planets.
There would be no more worlds to visit. Voyager 2 carried on the grand tour. Voyager 1 headed for the edge.
For nine more years it coasted outward. Then, on Valentine's Day 1990, it turned around for one last look.
From about six billion kilometers away, it shot a mosaic of dozens of frames, a family portrait of the planets.
In one frame, Earth is a speck smaller than a single pixel, caught in a beam of scattered sunlight.
The astronomer Carl Sagan called it a pale blue dot. Everyone who has ever lived, lived on that speck.
Soon after, the cameras were switched off for good, to save power for the long road ahead.
Our Sun blows a constant wind of charged particles. That wind inflates a giant bubble around the planets, called the heliosphere.
Outside the bubble is interstellar space, the thin gas between the stars.
On August 25th, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed that boundary. It was the first human-made object ever to do it.
But nobody could tell right away. Its plasma sensor, built to measure that gas, had stopped working long before.
Then in 2013, an outburst from the Sun made the gas around the probe ring like a bell.
The plasma wave instrument heard the tone. Its pitch revealed gas about forty times denser than inside the bubble.
Working backward, the team placed the crossing in August 2012. Voyager 1 had left the Sun's bubble behind.
Out here, sunlight is far too weak for solar panels. So Voyager runs on heat.
Three radioisotope generators sit on a long boom. Inside, plutonium slowly decays and stays hot.
Thermocouples turn that heat straight into electricity. No moving parts, nothing to wear out except time.
At launch, the three generators made about four hundred and seventy watts together.
But plutonium decays, and the converters age. Every year, Voyager loses about four watts of power.
So every year, the team must decide what to switch off next.
Heaters were turned down. The cameras went dark long ago. Then, one by one, the science instruments.
In February 2025, they switched off the cosmic ray experiment. In April 2026, the low energy particle instrument.
Today Voyager 1 runs just two science instruments, a magnetometer and the plasma wave instrument.
And its brains are pure 1970s. All its computers together hold about sixty-eight kilobytes of memory.
They run about eight thousand instructions per second. Yet this hardware has flown for almost fifty years.
Then, on November 14th, 2023, Voyager 1 started talking nonsense.
It still received commands, and it still seemed healthy. But the data coming home was a repeating pattern that meant nothing.
The trouble was in the flight data system, the computer that packages the probe's data before sending it home.
Voyager was about twenty-four billion kilometers away. Every command took about twenty-two and a half hours to arrive, and the reply took just as long.
In March 2024, the team coaxed the computer into sending back a readout of its own memory.
They found the culprit. A single memory chip had failed, wiping out a small slice of the computer's code.
You cannot swap a chip twenty-four billion kilometers away. So the team decided to move the code instead.
No single free spot was big enough. So they cut the code into pieces, tucked each piece somewhere else, and rewired every link between them.
On April 18th, 2024, they sent the first patch. Then they waited almost two days for an answer.
On April 20th, it came back. Readable engineering data, for the first time in five months.
By June, every working science instrument was sending usable data again. A 1977 computer had been rewired by remote control.
All of this depends on a whisper. Voyager's transmitter is only about as powerful as a refrigerator light bulb.
By the time that signal reaches Earth, NASA says it is one tenth of a billionth of a trillionth of a watt.
To catch it, NASA uses the Deep Space Network, giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia, spread around the globe.
The biggest dishes are seventy meters across. Their receivers are cooled to cut electronic noise.
Day after day, they pull Voyager's faint voice out of the hiss of the universe.
But the power keeps falling. So engineers came up with a bold move they call the Big Bang.
Switch several power-hungry systems to lower-power options, all at once. In 2026 it freed nearly ten watts on Voyager 2, and Voyager 1 is next.
Still, the end is coming. NASA thinks the probes could stay within reach until about 2036, if the power holds.
One day there will not be enough power to run the transmitter. The last signal will arrive, and then silence.
But Voyager will keep flying. Bolted to its side is a gold-plated copper record.
It carries greetings in fifty-five languages, sounds of Earth, and ninety minutes of music, for anyone who might find it.
In about forty thousand years, Voyager 1 will drift within about one point seven light-years of another star.
And right about now, Voyager 1 is crossing one light-day from home. A message sent today, at the speed of light, arrives tomorrow.
It took nearly forty-nine years to cover the distance light crosses in a single day. That is how big the dark is.
Still out there. Still listening. One light-day from home.
